title: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems” (from p. 664), p. 673. Scope: generalized arithmetic (Collatz-like) iteration systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-11: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.91

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim gives a constructive reduction between precise discrete systems. Its resolution requires checking the construction, not collecting new observations.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Verify an encoding of register-machine configurations as integers and prove that each remainder-selected arithmetic update simulates the corresponding register instruction. Universality follows from the established universality of the simulated register-machine model.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The exact allowed arithmetic rule family must be fixed.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The system is a concrete integer map with a stated correspondence to register-machine steps, the same idea as FRACTRAN. Traces can be compared for as many steps as one wants, and the reduction to a universal register machine is finite. That is a constructive proof, checkable by a short program.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Encode a register-machine state as an integer of the published form and apply the remainder-selected arithmetic map. Confirm if successive integers track the program counter and both registers for a universal register machine; refute if the map diverges from that trace. Universality then follows from the known universality of register machines.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The encoding uses a particular modulus and prime powers, so a checker has to test that program, not an arbitrary Collatz-like map.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.85
operationalizability: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.9
data existence: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For any two-register machine in Wolfram's sense (program of L instructions, each 'increment register r and go to the next instruction' or 'if register r is nonzero decrement it and jump to instruction j, else go to the next instruction', cyclic program), there is an arithmetic system n -> (p*n + q)/s whose branch is chosen by n mod 6L such that, with the state (i, a, b) encoded as n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b (Wolfram's encoding on p. 673 with L = 5 and modulus 30), the integer trajectory decodes step for step to the register machine's trajectory.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py compiles each two-register machine (program length L) into a table of 6L branches (p, q, s), one per residue n mod 6L, of the form n -> (p*n + q)/s with p, s in {1, 2, 3}: increments multiply the 2^a 3^b part by 2 or 3, decrements of a nonzero register divide it by 2 or 3 (the residue mod 6L tells whether the register is nonzero), and the additive constant moves the program position. Register machine and arithmetic map were run side by side in exact Python integers: 200 random L = 5 programs (numpy seed 20261111) from two starting states each for 10000 steps, and three hand-written growth programs (L = 3, 5, 7; moduli 18, 30, 42) for 20000 steps. At every step the integer n was compared with the encoding i + L * 2^a * 3^b of the simulated machine state (equivalent to decoding, since the encoding is injective). A perturbed map with one additive constant changed by one was run as a check that the comparison can fail.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. analysis.py compiles each register machine into the remainder-selected arithmetic map, then runs machine and map side by side. Test set: (a) all 200 register machines drawn with numpy seed 20261111 from the family with L = 5 and two registers (instruction type, register and jump target uniform), each from the state (1, 0, 0) and from one random state with registers in [0, 20], for 10000 steps; (b) three hand-written programs with L in {3, 5, 7} that move or copy register contents so that the registers grow without bound, 20000 steps each. 'supports' if at every step of every run the decoded (i, a, b) equals the directly simulated register-machine state (0 mismatches out of all compared steps) and, as a check that the comparison can fail, a deliberately perturbed map (one branch's additive constant changed by 1) produces a mismatch within 10000 steps on at least one of the hand-written programs. Universality of the arithmetic systems then follows from the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not tested.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run of the correctly compiled map disagrees with the register machine at any step. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the perturbation check fails to produce a mismatch (the comparison would then be too weak to count).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: steps at which the arithmetic-system value differs from the encoding of the register-machine state

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'system that takes a whole number, computes Mod[n, 30], and applies one of several arithmetic operations chosen by that remainder' is the family of generalised Collatz maps n -> (p*n + q)/s with the branch chosen by n mod M. The specific register machine of Wolfram's figure is not transcribed in the online text, so instead of checking his single example the test checks the general construction he describes (encoding n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b, modulus 6L; for L = 5 this is his modulus 30) on a random sample of register machines plus growth programs. Register-machine conventions follow NKS Chapter 3 (pp. 97-102): decrement of a zero register is a no-op that moves to the next instruction, and the program wraps around cyclically. The 'therefore universal' clause is a theorem of Minsky's and is outside what this computation establishes.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Two-register machines (NKS Chapter 3 conventions) and their compiled remainder-selected arithmetic maps, generated by analysis.py: 200 random programs of length 5 (numpy seed 20261111), three hand-written growth programs of length 3, 5 and 7; 10000 or 20000 steps per run; exact Python integers

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
What was verified is the emulation half of the claim: the described class of arithmetic systems (remainder modulo 6L selects one of 6L affine-rational operations) tracks arbitrary two-register machines exactly, over 4.06 million compared steps with register values up to several thousand and integers up to 14695 bits. The construction is general (it works for every program in the family, with L = 5 giving Wolfram's modulus 30), not a transcription of the particular 5-instruction machine in Wolfram's figure, whose program is not in the online text.

The 'therefore universal' clause rests on the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not re-proved; the compiled maps inherit universality from it only if one accepts that theorem. The closing remark that universality in arithmetic is unsurprising is an opinion and was not tested.

Finite traces cannot prove the emulation for all time, but the branch table is derived symbolically from the instruction semantics, so the trace check is a consistency test of that derivation rather than a sample-based estimate.

Register-machine conventions (cyclic program, decrement of zero is a no-op) follow NKS Chapter 3; a different convention would change the compiled table but not the construction.
